lessons.title: Corners First!
objectives: Use strategies to complete a simple jigsaw
Keep trying calmly when a piece doesn't fit
explanation: A jigsaw puzzle is a picture cut into pieces that fit together. A good strategy is to find the corner pieces first — they have two straight edges.
Next, find the edge pieces with one straight side and build the frame. Then fill the middle by matching colours and shapes.
If a piece doesn't fit, turn it around or try another spot. Being stuck is part of solving puzzles. Puzzle solvers stay calm and keep trying!

vocabulary.meaning: a picture cut into fitting pieces

examples: Finding the four corner pieces first.
Matching blue sky pieces together.

story.title: The Last Piece
story.text: Ivaan and Aaji worked on a jungle jigsaw. Corners first, then edges, then the tiger in the middle. But one piece wouldn't fit anywhere! Ivaan felt grumpy. Aaji said, "Let's turn it." He turned it once... twice... CLICK! It fit perfectly — the tiger's eye. "Stuck just means not yet," Aaji smiled.

lessons.title: Through the Maze
objectives: Find a path through a simple maze
Go back and try again at a dead end
prerequisites: Can follow a line with a finger
explanation: A maze is a puzzle made of paths. You start at one place and try to reach the finish.
Some paths lead to dead ends, where you can't go any further. When that happens, go back to the last place you had a choice and try another way.
A clever trick: try starting from the finish and working backwards! People have built mazes in gardens and hedges for hundreds of years.

A hedge maze in a garden.

story.title: The Mouse and the Cheese
story.text: In the puzzle book, a little mouse wanted to reach the cheese. Ivaan traced the path with his finger — left, down... dead end! He went back to the last turn and tried right. Up, around, down... CHEESE! "Want to know a trick?" asked Papa. "Start at the cheese and go backwards." Ivaan tried the next maze that way. It was super quick!

lessons.title: Spot the Difference
objectives: Find differences between two pictures by scanning carefully
Use strategies to remember where cards are
explanation: In spot-the-difference puzzles, two pictures look the same but have small changes. Good spotters scan carefully, part by part — top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right.
In the pairs (memory) game, cards are placed face down. You turn two over; if they match, you keep them. Remembering where cards are helps you win.
Saying things to yourself can help memory: "The cat is in the corner, the car is next to it." Paying attention is a skill we can practise.

examples: Finding the missing button in the second picture.

Bottom left — a missing flower! He found all five differences. "Slow looking is fast finding," he told his sister.

lessons.title: Seven Magic Pieces
objectives: Name the seven tangram pieces
Make pictures by turning and flipping pieces
explanation: A tangram is a Chinese puzzle made of seven flat pieces: five triangles (two big, one medium, two small), one square and one parallelogram.
Together, the seven pieces make a big square. But you can rearrange them to make hundreds of shapes — cats, boats, people, houses — using all seven pieces without overlapping.
To fit pieces, try turning (rotating) or flipping them over. Tangrams became popular around the world in the 1800s.
examples: A tangram cat with a triangle tail.
A tangram boat with a triangle sail.

story.title: The Tangram Swan
story.text: Zuri tipped out seven pieces. "Make a swan," said her uncle, showing a picture. She tried and tried — the neck wouldn't work. Then she flipped the parallelogram over, and suddenly it made a perfect curved neck! "Seven pieces, one swan," she smiled, and then made a cat, a rocket and a dancing person.

lessons.title: Sudoku and Magic Squares
objectives: Solve a 4×4 sudoku using logic
Check and complete a 3×3 magic square
explanation: In a 4×4 sudoku, each row, each column and each 2×2 box must contain the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 exactly once. You use logic, not guessing: "This row already has 1, 2 and 4, so the empty square must be 3."
A magic square is a grid where every row, column and diagonal adds up to the same number. In the classic 3×3 magic square using 1 to 9, the magic sum is 15.

The Lo Shu square from ancient Chinese legend is a 3×3 magic square. Magic squares also appear in India — a 4×4 magic square is carved at the Parshvanath temple in Khajuraho, dated to around the 10th century.

vocabulary.meaning: a grid where all lines add to the same sum

examples: Rows of the Lo Shu: 4 9 2, 3 5 7, 8 1 6.
The Khajuraho magic square, where every row and column adds to 34.

story.title: The Turtle's Shell
story.text: An old Chinese legend tells that during a great flood, a turtle emerged from the river with a strange pattern of dots on its shell. The dots formed numbers 1 to 9 in a square where every line added to 15. People saw it as a sign of order and harmony, and named it the Lo Shu.

lessons.title: What Am I?
objectives: Solve riddles by thinking about clues and double meanings
Create original riddles
explanation: A riddle is a question or statement that needs clever thinking to solve. Many riddles describe something in a surprising way: "I have hands but cannot clap. What am I?" (A clock!)
Riddles often use double meanings — words that mean two things. A clock's "hands" are not real hands.
Riddles appear in stories everywhere: the Sphinx's riddle in Greek myth, Betal's riddles to King Vikramaditya, and the Yaksha's questions to Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata.

vocabulary.meaning: a puzzling question needing clever thinking
a word that means two things

examples: "What has keys but can't open locks?" — a piano.
"What gets wetter the more it dries?" — a towel.

story.title: The Yaksha's Questions
story.text: In the Mahabharata, a Yaksha guarding a lake asked Yudhishthira many riddles before letting him drink. "What is faster than the wind?" "The mind." "What is more numerous than grass?" "Thoughts." Yudhishthira answered wisely, and the Yaksha restored his brothers to life.

lessons.title: Four Steps to Solving
objectives: Apply Polya's four steps to a problem
Choose strategies like drawing, working backwards and simplifying
explanation: Mathematician George Polya, in "How to Solve It" (1945), described four steps: Understand the problem; Devise a plan; Carry out the plan; Look back (check and reflect).
Useful strategies include: draw a diagram, make a table, look for a pattern, work backwards, try a simpler version, and guess and check.
Looking back is often skipped but powerful: Does the answer make sense? Could I solve it another way? Can I use this method again?

vocabulary.meaning: think back on what you did

examples: Drawing a diagram for a handshake problem.
Working backwards from the end of a story problem.

story.title: The Handshake Problem
story.text: Ten friends each shake hands once with every other friend. How many handshakes? Kiko started counting and got confused. Then he tried a simpler version: 2 friends — 1. 3 friends — 3. 4 friends — 6. A pattern! 1, 3, 6, 10... For 10 friends: 45. He checked with a formula: 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45. Looking back, he grinned.

lessons.title: Wolf, Goat and Cabbage
objectives: Solve a river-crossing puzzle systematically
Use a logic grid to solve clue puzzles
explanation: In a classic river-crossing puzzle, a farmer must take a wolf, a goat and a cabbage across a river in a boat that holds only the farmer and one item. The wolf can't be left alone with the goat, nor the goat with the cabbage.

The solution: take the goat across; return; take the wolf across; bring the goat back; take the cabbage across; return; take the goat across. The key insight is that you can bring something back! Such puzzles appear in a manuscript attributed to Alcuin of York, around 800 CE.
Logic grid puzzles give clues about people and their choices; you mark a grid with ✓ and ✗ to eliminate possibilities until only one answer remains.
examples: The farmer bringing the goat back across.
A grid showing who owns which pet.

story.title: The Farmer's Puzzle

Zuri's eyes lit up — she brought the goat back across, and suddenly the puzzle solved itself. "Going backwards was the answer!"

lessons.title: Towers and Bridges
objectives: Find and explain the minimum moves for the Tower of Hanoi
Use Euler's reasoning about the Königsberg bridges
explanation: The Tower of Hanoi, invented by Édouard Lucas in 1883, has discs on one peg to be moved to another, one at a time, never placing a larger disc on a smaller one. With n discs, the minimum number of moves is 2ⁿ − 1: 3 discs take 7 moves; 4 discs take 15.
In 1736, Leonhard Euler studied the seven bridges of Königsberg: could you walk across each bridge exactly once? He proved it was impossible, founding graph theory.
Euler showed that a path crossing every edge once exists only if zero or two points (vertices) have an odd number of connections. Königsberg had four land areas, all with an odd number of bridges.

vocabulary.meaning: the study of networks of points and lines
a path using every edge exactly once

examples: Tower of Hanoi with 3 discs in 7 moves.

story.title: The Bridges of Königsberg
story.text: Citizens of Königsberg loved Sunday walks across the seven bridges of their river. They wondered whether anyone could cross each bridge exactly once. Nobody succeeded. In 1736, Leonhard Euler turned the map into dots and lines and proved it impossible. A puzzle about a Sunday walk became a new branch of mathematics.

lessons.title: Thinking Outside the Box
objectives: Solve lateral thinking puzzles by questioning assumptions
Apply creative thinking techniques
explanation: Lateral thinking, a term coined by Edward de Bono in 1967, means solving problems by approaching them from unexpected angles rather than step-by-step logic alone.

The nine dots puzzle asks you to join nine dots in a 3×3 grid with four straight lines without lifting your pen. Most people fail because they assume lines must stay inside the square. Going outside the dots solves it — possibly the origin of "thinking outside the box".
Techniques include questioning assumptions, reversing the problem, using random prompts and asking "what if?". Good problem solvers combine logical and lateral thinking.
examples: The nine dots puzzle.
Asking "How could we make this problem worse?" to find solutions.

story.text: A classic puzzle: a man lives on the 10th floor. Every morning he takes the lift down. In the evening, he takes the lift to the 7th floor and walks up — unless it's raining or others are in the lift. Why? Meera puzzled over it, then questioned her assumption that he was tall. "He's too short to reach the 10th button — unless he has an umbrella!"

lessons.title: The Prisoner's Dilemma
objectives: Analyse the prisoner's dilemma and Nash equilibrium
Evaluate how cooperation can emerge in repeated games
explanation: Game theory studies strategic decisions where each person's outcome depends on others' choices. It was developed by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern (1944) and extended by John Nash.

In the prisoner's dilemma, two suspects are questioned separately. If both stay silent, both get short sentences. If one betrays the other, the betrayer goes free and the other gets a long sentence. If both betray, both get medium sentences. Each is individually better off betraying — so both betray, though both would be better off cooperating. Mutual betrayal is a Nash equilibrium: no one gains by changing strategy alone.

In repeated games, cooperation can emerge. In Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments (around 1980), the simple strategy "tit for tat" — cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move — performed remarkably well.

vocabulary.meaning: a state where no player benefits from changing strategy alone
cooperate first, then copy the other player

examples: Two shops in a price war.
Countries negotiating climate agreements.

story.title: The Tournament
story.text: In 1980, political scientist Robert Axelrod invited experts to submit computer programs to play repeated prisoner's dilemma against each other. Complex, clever strategies entered. The winner was the shortest program: tit for tat, submitted by Anatol Rapoport. Nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear — it suggested how cooperation might evolve.

lessons.title: Unsolved Mysteries of Mathematics
objectives: Describe famous solved and unsolved mathematical problems
Evaluate what drives mathematical discovery
explanation: Some problems take centuries. Fermat's Last Theorem (that aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no whole-number solutions for n > 2) was stated around 1637 and proved by Andrew Wiles in 1994. The Four Colour Theorem was proved in 1976 with computer help.

Many puzzles remain open. The Collatz conjecture: start with any positive whole number; if even, halve it; if odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Does every number eventually reach 1? Nobody knows. The Riemann Hypothesis, about prime numbers, is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a one-million-dollar prize.

Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920), largely self-taught, filled notebooks with remarkable formulas; mathematicians are still exploring them. His story with G. H. Hardy, and the "taxicab number" 1729, show the joy of puzzles at the highest level. India celebrates National Mathematics Day on his birthday, 22 December.

vocabulary.meaning: a statement believed true but not yet proved
a logical argument showing something is true
a number with exactly two factors

story.title: The Taxicab Number
story.text: When G. H. Hardy visited Ramanujan in hospital, he said his taxi's number, 1729, seemed dull. "No," Ramanujan replied at once, "it is a very interesting number. It is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways." 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³. Numbers, for Ramanujan, were old friends.
